news.title: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
news.summary: Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame. So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems.

news.title: USC engineers built a smart ring that detects stress with light
news.summary: Stress tracking on wearables like the Fitbit Sense usually relies on electrodermal activity, or EDA. The method measures changes in skin conductance caused by sweat glands, but it needs electrodes to stay in steady contact with your skin. Conductive gels can dry out, and movement can throw off the readings over long stretches. A University of Southern California team led by assistant professor Yasser Khan and his PhD student Farhad Hassan built an AI-powered ring that uses near-infrared light to track sweat activity beneath the skin. Their findings were published in Science Advances. USC Khan Lab Stress activates your sweat glands and causes subtle changes under the skin before visible sweat appears.

In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far. news.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models
news.summary: Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. news.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
news.summary: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

news.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
news.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.

news.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
news.summary: Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs.In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes.They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch.In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy.This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud.“There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September.

news.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
news.summary: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping.

news.title: Microsoft Launches MAI Licensed Weights AI Models With Frontier-Level Performance
news.summary: More of what makes a company distinctive will live inside the AI models it runs. Businesses increasingly want to control those models: who can access them, how they’re adapted, what they cost to operate, and when they’re upgraded. That’s why we’re introducing MAI Licensed Weights, giving organizations the ability to deploy and customize Microsoft AI models in their own Azure environments. MAI Licensed Weights brings Microsoft’s frontier AI models into your own Azure environment, where you can adapt them to your business and safely integrate your proprietary knowledge and expertise. Your data and adaptations remain yours, with Microsoft only using them to train its models with your express agreement. As these models become embedded in your most important products and workflows, you retain control over how they’re deployed, who can access them, and when they’re upgraded.

news.title: Microsoft Launches MAI Cyber 2 Flash: Frontier-Level Security AI at Lower Cost
news.summary: Security teams need AI to find vulnerabilities, recommend fixes, and investigate threats around the clock. Doing that at scale takes serious computing power, and the cost can quickly add up. Built on Microsoft’s decades of proprietary security data and expertise, MAI Cyber 2 Flash is our latest specialist security model. It delivers leading performance on real-world security tasks at a fraction of the cost of larger models. And we’re bringing that capability directly into Microsoft’s security products. On CyberGym‑E2E1, a benchmark measuring real-world vulnerability discovery, MAI Cyber 2 Flash (92.3%) beats GPT-6 Astra (91.5%)5 at less than 2% of the cost per task.3 It also outperforms GPT-5.6 Cyber6 on CyberGym‑E2E and WebExploitBench at the same reasoning budget.2

news.title: Microsoft Launches MAI Code 2 & Code 2 Flash: Scalable AI Coding Models
news.summary: MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash: two new coding models built for everyday enterprise coding tasks, delivering leading performance at a fraction of the cost of competing models. MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo-wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost. Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long-horizon agentic work.

news.title: Google AI Mode Adds Temporary Threads for Private, History-Free Searches
news.summary: We’re introducing temporary threads in AI Mode, where you can explore and ask questions — whether that’s brainstorming a surprise gift or looking something up you don’t want resurfaced later like in your history or recommendations. There’s no need to adjust your settings — you can quickly jump into a temporary thread for any query you don't want saved, and switch right back when you're done. To get started, simply click the temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode and start asking your questions. Because your session is completely detached from your account, your responses won’t be informed by past preferences, affect future personalization, or be saved to your history. Once you close the thread, it’s gone, letting you go back to searching as usual. This feature is rolling out globally on desktop and mobile browsers across all languages supported in AI Mode.

news.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
news.summary: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. news.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
news.summary: Nvidia-fueled crackdown US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.” The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register.
